title: How structures and systems help learning happen (or not) - 3
author: Martin Skelton
summary: The final post on structures and systems argues that well-designed systems help learning in three further ways. They define where individuality is free and where shared practice is needed, they save time for learning, and they build community confidence. Skelton illustrates with his experience of launching a group of 40 schools with minimal rules, and with stories of a head who made teachers copy out their plans by hand and of two maths classrooms with very different help-seeking routines. He also contrasts two schools' parent consultation evenings. The post ends with an eight-question checklist for auditing classroom and school systems through a learning lens.
points: Clearly stated shared systems also mark out where teachers may exercise freedom, so consistency need not mean robotic uniformity.
Wasteful structures, such as hand-copying plans already in a folder, drain the time teachers need to think about learning.
A simple classroom protocol for what to do when stuck can recover substantial learning time that raised-hand queues lose.
A consistent, learning-focused format for parent consultations builds community confidence and reduces anxiety.
Structures are themselves repeated experiences that teach everyone what the school really values, and so deserve regular audit.
quotes: By making clear what needs to be collaborative because it gives the best chance of supporting student learning, it also makes clear where individual behaviours can flourish. The paradox here is that by defining clearly the learning-focused systems and structures that need to be shared and consented to, a school is also defining the areas in which everyone has personal freedom and which also support the development of interdependence and independence.

At the very beginning, we said this to our school leaders and, particularly, to our teacher colleagues: As long as your students are treated respectfully, as long as you model respectful behaviour with other teachers and parents, as long as your students treat each other with respect, as long as you know what you want them to get better at on a weekly, termly and yearly basis, and as long as you can show evidence that they are getting better as a result of the repeated experiences you create, then we don’t mind what you do as a teacher.

Making sure that a school’s learning-focused structures, systems and processes are clear and have the consent of everyone in the school does two things simultaneously. It lets everyone know when and where they have to play the collective game and, to their benefit and to the benefit of the children and students in the school, where they don’t.

For reasons best known to himself, the Head had devised a system and structure for all of his teaching staff that - by asking the staff, each day and each week, to copy out something they already had in their rooms - made teachers tired, unreflective about learning, waste time and become sceptical about what they were doing in the school.

As I get alongside these students, it becomes clear that almost all of the learning breakdown is being caused because the students have individually forgotten relatively simple procedural points about the math they are doing. I ask one of the students why they don’t check in with the student sitting next to them. I am told that they aren’t allowed to do that and they must wait to be seen by their teacher.

What these people say to each other about a school when they meet at the gate, at the weekends and in each other’s houses is a repeated experience that is going to create, fairly or unfairly, the reputation of the school and stakeholder confidence in it.

As structures, systems and processes are, in themselves, repeated experiences they don’t only affect learning they cause learning to happen. They help everyone in the school learn what really matters.
